one_liner: Header-only C++23 hyper-dual numbers giving value, gradient and dense Hessian in one pass; 1.2-3.3x faster than Eigen AutoDiffScalar/autodiff.
what_it_does: Forward-mode algorithmic differentiation where each scalar carries its value, gradient and (for second order) the packed upper triangle of the Hessian, so evaluating a templated function once yields all second derivatives. DDScalar<Order, T, N> comes in static-size (N fixed at compile time, std::array storage) and dynamic-size (std::vector) variants; SScalar/SSScalar key derivatives by variable name for assembly-style code. You write the function over a template scalar type, as with ceres::Jet or Eigen AutoDiffScalar, and read f(), g(i), h(i,j); pybind11 Python bindings expose the same types with a native NumPy dtype for static sizes.
how_it_is_fast: Hyper-dual (truncated second-order Taylor) arithmetic propagates the gradient and Hessian through each operation via the chain rule, so the Hessian comes from one evaluation rather than nested first-order duals (Eigen AutoDiffScalar of AutoDiffScalar) or n(n+1)/2 re-evaluations (autodiff dual2nd's hessian()). The Hessian is stored as a packed upper triangle in a fixed-size std::array, all operators are force-inlined, and constant partials (zero, one, minus one) are compile-time tags that fold away. Above 8 variables the gradient and Hessian are updated in one fused pass over the data array, a threshold the source comments say was measured on an M1 Pro (n=16 35% faster fused, n=6 14% slower).
when_to_use: Element-level Hessians in nonlinear finite-element, isogeometric or cable/shell mechanics codes, where each element has a small, compile-time-known number of DOFs (roughly 3-24).
Newton-type solvers that need exact local Hessians of small dense functions evaluated many times (strain energies, constitutive laws).
Python prototyping of second-derivative code: static types back a NumPy dtype, which the README measured at 52x-246x faster than dtype=object arrays for elementwise ops.
Assembly code that wants derivatives keyed by variable name and projected onto a caller-chosen global ordering (SSScalar g(names)/hm(names)).
when_not_to_use: Gradient-only work: the README's own first-order table shows no gain over Eigen AutoDiffScalar (244 vs 245 ns at n=24), and Ceres Jet comes with a solver.

Variable counts unknown at compile time: the dynamic variant allocates per operation and was 43x slower than static at n=3, and slower than both Eigen AutoDiffScalar nested and autodiff dual2nd at every tested size in the second-order table.

Many inputs or large n: forward-mode cost and the dense Hessian grow quadratically, and the speedup already narrows to 1.5x at n=24; reverse-mode tools (Adept, XAD) suit scalar functions of hundreds of inputs.
Toolchains older than GCC 14 / Clang 18 / MSVC 19.38: the header uses C++23 explicit object parameters ('deducing this').
Projects needing third derivatives or sparse Hessians within a set of variables: only first and second order are provided, and SSScalar's Hessian is dense over the names it carries.

integration.dependencies: none for C++ (standard library only); Python bindings need pybind11, scikit-build-core and NumPy >= 2.0
integration.min_toolchain: C++23; GCC 14+, Clang 18+, MSVC 19.38+ (README); CMake 3.14+ for the provided target
integration.platforms: any (portable C++; benchmarks only on Apple M1 Pro)
integration.thread_safety: not documented (scalars are value types with no shared state in the header)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same template-scalar style as Eigen AutoDiffScalar or ceres::Jet, so a templated function can switch types, but the accessors (f(), g(i), h(i,j), variables()) differ and Eigen-specific traits are not provided.

gotchas: pip install hyperjet installs 1.5.0 from August 2023, not the benchmarked C++23 code; the README's CPM line pins HyperJet@2.0.0, but the tags page shows no 2.0.0 tag (latest v1.5.0), so pin a commit on main to get the rewrite (C++23 switch landed May 2026, benchmark July 2026).
C++ accessors g(i), h(i), h(i,j) are only checked by assert in debug builds; constructors and resize/eval paths throw std::runtime_error unless HYPERJET_NO_EXCEPTIONS is defined.
References returned by data() from a temporary expression are valid only within the full expression, as with std::vector::operator[].

Performance depends on inlining: the README measured a 1.56x penalty for HyperJet (similar for Eigen and Ceres) when the enclosing expression is not inlined, and writing acc += term instead of acc = acc + term saved 8% at n=24.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick HyperJet over Adept-2, XAD or FastAD when you need exact dense Hessians of small fixed-size functions, since those tape-based tools target first-order reverse mode over many inputs (Adept has no higher-order mode). Sleipnir bundles its own AD with an NLP solver and Enzyme needs an LLVM plugin; neither is a lightweight per-element Hessian scalar.
verified_claims_summary: The author's Google Benchmark harness (benchmark/compare/compare.cpp, Apple clang 21.0.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG on an Apple M1 Pro, Eigen 3.4.0, autodiff v1.1.2, Ceres 2.2.0) times value, gradient and dense Hessian of a cable strain-energy sum: static HyperJet takes 15/101/921/12,214 ns at n=3/6/12/24 against 18/328/2,888/22,105 ns for nested Eigen AutoDiffScalar and 127/375/2,425/17,679 ns for autodiff dual2nd, after checking all contenders agree bit-for-bit. For gradients alone it ties Eigen AutoDiffScalar and is about 1.25x faster than ceres::Jet at n=24.
status_note: Actively developed by a single author (C++23 rewrite in May 2026, last commit 2026-07-28, 17 stars) under MIT, small enough to vendor as one header, but the rewritten version has no tagged release or PyPI package yet.
